To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pretreatment of the kidney donor with cytotoxic drugs markedly reduced the immunogenicity of the kidney allograft and that the isolated organ perfused preparation was an effective way to deliver the drugs to the graft.
the pretreatment of donors with cytotoxic drugs markedly reduces allograft rejection.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunogenetic basis of the rejection reaction of renal allografts in the rat and its modification by cytotoxic drugs.
the development of a model for studying renal transplantation in the rat.
the immunologic mechanisms of renal allograft rejection in a well-defined system of inbred rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunosuppressive drugs are effective in preventing rejection, and that this effect is not dependent on the presence of lymphoid cells in the graft.

, in this particular system, pretreatment of the donor of the renal allograft with high doses of the cytotoxic drugs cyclophosphoramide, methotrezate, or proearbazine results in a significant reduction of the immunogenicity of the kidney and thus a reduction in the degree of histoincompatibility.

, in the present series of experiments, the results of pretreatment of the donor with cyclophosphoramide, methotraxate, and procarbazine were similar, but that cyclophosphamidewas the best of the three agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immunologic basis of renal transplantation can be studied in a variety of inbred rat strains, but the immunologic barriers to successful grafting are so great that only the use of immunosuppressive drugs or other methods of suppressing the host's immunologic reactivity can lead to the successful transplantation of an allogeneic kidney.
the inbred rat is an excellent model for the study of the immunogenetic and immunological factors involved in organ transplantation.
the immunologic response in transplantation can be influenced by the immunologic status of the donor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the kidney can be transplanted across a major histocompatibility barrier, and that the kidney can survive and function for long periods of time in the recipient.
we are able to reduce the immunogenicity of the donor kidney by pretreating the kidney.

the use of a single dose of the drug cyclophosphomide (CYC) to treat the donor of an organ prior to its transplantation into the recipient is a safe and effective way to reduce the risk of organ rejection by the recipient.
